results.abstract_text:
PROJECT SUMMARY
Brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) have the potential to restore communication, motor, and sensory functions to
people living with paralysis from neurologic injury or disease. Rapid progress has been made over the past few
years, particularly with the ability to restore speech and communication, with numerous demonstrations of BCI
performance approaching able-bodied typing and speaking rates. In research studies, BCIs are being used in
home environments more often than ever and both decoding stability and performance are increasing rapidly.
Critically, a robust translational pipeline from academia to industry has emerged with major investments
accelerating efforts to bring BCI technology to market, including industry-led clinical trials. Success in the
academic BCI community has fundamentally derisked and enabled these advances. Continued advances and
successful translation of BCI technology into the clinic will depend on close and productive interactions that bring
all stakeholders together to focus on critical scientific and technical issues guided by user priorities. The
International BCI Meeting Series, which has included 11 meetings since 1999, has always had the goal of
bringing a broad range of disciplines together to discuss issues that are critical for BCI development to restore
communication and mobility. The BCI Meetings are instrumental in creating the productive collaborations that
are essential for progress. The 12th International BCI Meeting will be organized to achieve the following aims:
 1. Convene and foster productive interactions among all disciplines and stakeholders whose cooperation is
 crucial to successful BCI research and development. No other venue brings them all together.
 2. Present a concise and comprehensive update of the current state of BCI research and development,
 including ongoing clinical trials.
 3. Address topics critical for progress in BCI research and development through focused workshops and
 targeted plenary sessions. Broader topics will be covered in oral and poster presentations.
 4. Promote the education and development of graduate students and postdoctoral fellows. Networking
 events will encourage interactions between new and established researchers.
 5. Maximize the immediate and long-term meeting impact through publication of a special issue of peer-
 reviewed primary articles and focused reviews derived from the meeting. Open-access conference
 proceedings will inform both the scientific community and the general public.
In summary, the 12th International BCI Meeting will bring together all stakeholders from the BCI community,
review the state of the field including recent scientific, technical, and clinical advances, will address key issues
critical for translating research into clinical use, and will promote the education and mentoring of young
researchers. Like its predecessors, this meeting and the resulting publications will promote the advancement of
BCIs to restore communication and motor functions to people living with paralysis and other impairments.
results.phr_text:
PROJECT NARRATIVE
The International Brain-Computer Interface (BCI) Meeting Series is unique in providing an interdisciplinary,
collaborative environment that convenes representatives from all fields involved in BCI research, including
scientists, engineers, clinicians, policymakers, and users. The 12th International BCI Meeting will highlight
innovative approaches and applications for BCIs, highlight recent results from clinical trials, discuss progress
towards translation, and promote the education and participation of young researchers. This meeting and the
resulting comprehensive publications will, like its predecessors, foster the translation of BCIs into clinically viable
devices.

results.abstract_text:
ABSTRACT
The development of brain-controlled prosthetic arms promises to provide independence to people with paralysis.
To date, however, Brain-Computer Interfaces (BCIs) have not conferred on users the ability to use the prosthesis
to carry out activities of daily living (ADLs) with adequate reliability and flexibility. This inability can be traced
back to at least three shortcomings. First, while we naturally closely coordinate arm and hand movements,
current BCI users reach and grasp sequentially, in large part due to the way BCI decoders are built. Second,
existing decoders use the component of the neuronal activity that has a direct and immediate relationship with
motor output to infer motor intent. While this approach has been successful even for control of an
anthropomorphic robotic arm and hand, it does not harness all the behaviorally relevant M1 activity. Indeed,
activity that has a direct and immediate relationship with behavior – the so-called output-potent activity –
constitutes only a small fraction of the total M1 activity. The remaining neuronal activity – so-called output-null
activity – plays a role in generating the output-potent activity but is overlooked by standard decoding approaches.
Third, while robotic hands have become increasingly sophisticated and anthropomorphic, no existing prototype
approaches the functionality of a human hand, either in terms of actuation or sensorization.
 The goal of the proposed project is to address each of the aforementioned limitations by building more
biomimetic decoders – that allow for coordinated arm and hand movements and more effectively harness M1
activity – and by challenging them in a flexible and realistic virtual reality platform. First, we will build decoding
approaches that support coordinated movements of the arm and hand. To this end, we will train decoders while
subjects reach to and grasp objects that differ in shape, size, and orientation, forcing significant hand orienting
and pre-shaping during reaching. Second, we will further elaborate these decoders so that they leverage both
output-potent and output-null activity. To this end, we will leverage recent insights into M1 dynamics and their
relationship to behavior to build decoders that harness all the behaviorally relevant activity in M1. Finally, we will
test novel decoders in VR by having subjects perform standard tests of arm and hand function as well as tasks
that mimic complex activities of daily living and develop performance metrics for these VR scenarios. We are
well positioned to achieve these objectives as part of a multi-site clinical trial on BCI with 3 subjects implanted
across two locations, with existing funding for two more subjects.
results.project_title: Improved Brain-Computer Interface Decoding for Activities of Daily Life
results.phr_text:
PROJECT NARRATIVE
The development of brain-controlled prosthetic arms promises to provide independence to users, but current
efforts suffer from at least two limitations: first, they are limited in their ability to coordinate arm and hand
movements due to the way that decoders are trained, and second, they only harness a small fraction of the
activity in motor cortex to infer motor intent. We propose to address these two limitations by leveraging advances
in our basic understanding of motor control and by testing next-generation decoders in sophisticated and realistic
VR scenarios.

results.abstract_text:
Project Summary
Brain-Computer Interfaces (BCIs) enable direct communication between the brain and the external world. We
propose to establish and investigate the mechanisms of a novel, noninvasive bidirectional BCI (bi-BCI) platform.
This system combines electroencephalography (EEG)-based neural decoding (“reading” brain activity) with
closed-loop, low-intensity transcranial focused ultrasound (tFUS) neuromodulation (“writing” to the brain). This
dual approach enables real-time measurement of behavior via BCI decoding and adaptive modulation of neural
circuits. By integrating noninvasive neural decoding with precision neuromodulation, the proposed bi-BCI offers
a transformative platform for mechanistic studies of mind–body interventions—revealing how specific brain
activity patterns relate to behavior and how targeted modulation can shift these patterns to achieve desired
outcomes. To realize this vision, we propose two Specific Aims unified under a central theme: to develop and
investigate a bi-BCI framework that engages both the “mind” (intention and cognition) and “body” (physiological
processes) for two key applications—communication prostheses (Aim 1) and motor prostheses (Aim 2). This
foundational work will catalyze a new class of mind–body interventions. Aim 1: Establish a tFUS-integrated
motion-onset visual evoked potential BCI speller for communication and investigate neural mechanisms of
cognitive attention during mind–body interactions. We will enhance feature-based attention mechanisms by
combining motion-onset visual stimulation with targeted neuromodulation of visual area V5. This approach will
yield a novel bi-BCI with significantly improved accuracy and information throughput. Aim 2: Establish and
investigate a tFUS-modulated sensorimotor rhythm (SMR) bi-BCI using motor imagery for motor control. We will
test the hypothesis that tFUS modulates the dynamics of event-related desynchronization/synchronization
(ERD/ERS), thereby enhancing motor imagery-based BCI control of an external object. Successful completion
of this research will significantly enhance BCI performance and yield critical insights into the neural mechanisms
underlying mind–body interventions made possible by neuromodulation-enhanced, closed-loop bi-BCIs.
results.project_title: Bidirectional brain-computer interface with closed-loop mind-body interactions
results.phr_text:
NARRATIVE
The goal of this project is to establish and investigate the neural mechanisms underlying a noninvasive,
bidirectional brain-computer interface with closed-loop mind-body interactions. Successful completion of the
proposed research promises to significantly advance brain-controlled communication and assistive technologies
using a noninvasive approach—an area currently limited in capability. This work has the potential to benefit
numerous individuals with motor impairments and speech disorders, while also improving the well-being and
quality of life for many others.

results.abstract_text:
The performance of intracortical brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) has advanced substantially over the last
decade, but these devices are not yet robust enough for the home environment, where they can truly improve
quality of life for individuals with disabilities. To date, BCIs have depended on experienced technicians to operate
large and complicated systems comprised of multiple computers, signal processors, neural recording
headstages, and custom software. Our laboratory has developed a portable, battery-powered intracortical BCI
system that enables independent in-home computer access. However, to achieve the long-term goal of true
clinical viability, BCIs must also offer reliable and robust functional performance in the less well-controlled home
environment. We have achieved robust and generalizable control of a computer cursor using a biomimetic
approach that combines reach-based velocity control of cursor position with grasp-based control of mouse click
onset and offset. This transient-based neural decoder allows for generalized click function, adding the ability to
‘click-and-drag’ when accessing a computer (similar to carrying an object) to the ‘point-and-click’ functionality
that is typically implemented in BCIs. Independent home use of the BCI system will provide an opportunity to
collect neural data over long periods of time during unstructured and varied tasks, enabling quantification of
context-dependent neural variability due to subject-state (e.g., fatigue, pain, or stress) as well as plasticity due
to learning. Understanding how neural signals vary over time will be critical for clinical BCI systems that must be
robust, generalizable, and autonomous (i.e., operate for extended periods without technician intervention).
This project will first quantify the impact of subject-state on movement-related neural activity and performance
during in-home BCI use. This understanding is critical to developing robust BCIs that eliminate the need for
recalibration even in uncontrolled environments. The extent to which subject-state information is represented in
motor cortex and overlaps with BCI control dimensions will inform development efforts to mitigate the impact of
these nuisance variables. Participants will use the BCI for a variety of self-selected computer access tasks over
periods of many months that will challenge decoder performance. This project will investigate motor learning
mechanisms that may be engaged to facilitate improvements in performance that generalize to many different
tasks. Experiments will test the hypothesis that stable population-level neural activity emerges to strengthen
movement-related activity while minimizing non-task-related neural variability. Finally, participants will undergo
targeted neural training to determine if motor learning can be accelerated and whether different mechanisms of
neural reorganization are engaged in response to interventions that challenge the speed and accuracy properties
of the decoder in different ways. This project will improve our understanding of neural plasticity mechanisms
during extended BCI use in a real-world environment. Ultimately this knowledge will enable stable, high-
functioning BCI performance during independent home-use, which is critical for clinical translation.
results.project_title: Quantifying neural variability and learning during real world brain-computer interface use
results.phr_text:
PROJECT NARRATIVE
Brain-computer interfaces must enable robust and generalizable control of assistive devices in uncontrolled
environments, such as the home. Through this proposal, we will study how the physical or cognitive state of a
participant impact neural activity and system performance. In addition, we will characterize the extent to which
experience- or training-induced motor learning can drive neural plasticity and improve BCI robustness.

PROJECT SUMMARY / ABSTRACT
The objective of this project is to develop an advanced brain-computer interface (BCI) that restores speech to
people with paralysis. The long-term goal of this research is to improve quality of life for people with
communication loss due to neurological disorders such as amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) or stroke.
 Current speech BCIs translate users’ neural activity into text as they attempt to speak. This approach
works by mapping neural activity to phonemes, and then applying a series of machine learning models to
transform phonemes to words. By design, this approach is restricted in its ability to generalize beyond text
output. The alternative approach proposed in this application is to train decoders that decode the user’s
articulatory movements instead of directly decoding sentences. This project will test the hypothesis that
paralyzed users will be able to use a kinematics-based BCI designed this way to accurately control virtual
orofacial components (lips, tongue, etc.), and that the decoded vocal tract configuration will be able to be
converted in real-time into expressive speech sounds on behalf of the user.
 The methods used will build on prior work, utilizing the same neural recording techniques (intracortical
microelectrode arrays), brain region (ventral precentral gyrus, i.e., speech motor cortex), and participants
(BrainGate2 clinical trial participants who have ALS or stroke). The first aim is to determine whether speech
motor cortex supports closed-loop control of individual speech articulators by implementing a lips BCI
controllable by participants with paralysis. The second aim is to characterize the neural encoding of speech
and basic tongue movements, to determine whether neural decoders trained on simple instructed movement
cues will generalize to similar movements made in the context of speech. These aims are not mutually
dependent, and the success of either aim will lead to a fundamental insight to the function of the human brain.
 This research will take place in the Neuroprosthetics Lab at UC Davis, one of four BrainGate2 clinical
trial sites across the U.S. This fellowship training plan focuses on key areas of growth required to conduct the
proposed research and to prepare for a productive research career in BCI: speech BCI development,
phonetics, computational neuroscience, scientific communication, leadership, and career development. A team
of 5 qualified mentors (all UC Davis faculty) will provide guidance and expertise throughout this training plan.
 This work aims to elevate quality of life for people with speech loss by enabling a rich, expressive mode
of communication using intracortical BCIs. Additionally, this project will shed light on fundamental neuroscience
questions regarding speech production and neuromotor control.
results.project_title: An articulatory brain-computer interface approach for restoring expressive communication to people with paralysis
results.phr_text:
PROJECT NARRATIVE
This project seeks to expand our understanding of the brain functions underlying speech production in order to
improve quality of life for people with paralysis and communication loss due to neurological disorders such as
amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and stroke. This proposal will test the hypothesis that decoding speech
articulatory movement commands from the motor cortex will provide a novel approach for improving
brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) for restoring speech. A speech BCI inspired by the innate flexibility of able
speakers’ physical vocal tracts could dramatically improve the accuracy and expressiveness of paralyzed
users’ communication abilities, restoring a fundamental human need.
